extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, press-freedom advocates, researchers interested in government treatment of the press
extracted.subtask_description: A chronological, Wikipedia-style compilation documenting incidents, legal responses, and reactions relating to government attacks on journalists in the United States. Includes references to statutes, court precedent, advocacy responses, and remedial actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act (FACE Act) — 18 U.S.C. §248
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits the use of force, threat of force, or physical obstruction to interfere with a person's exercise of religious worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited in the article as one of the federal statutes prosecutors considered when evaluating whether to bring charges (e.g., in the post-protest charges discussed for Don Lemon).

rubrics_metrics.name: 18 U.S.C. §241 (civil rights conspiracy statute)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Reconstruction-era civil rights conspiracy statute (commonly associated with the Ku Klux Klan Act) criminalizing conspiracies to violate civil rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as another federal statute prosecutors considered when deciding on potential charges arising from protest-related incidents involving journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bartnicki v. Vopper (2001) — disclosure protection precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Established protections for 'a person's right to disclose illegally intercepted communications if they were not part of the illegal interception itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the article to explain legal protections that may apply to journalists who publish leaked or intercepted communications; relevant background in accounts of raids/seizures of journalist materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy Protection Act of 1980
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires the government to obtain a subpoena to obtain journalist work products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited in the context of the FBI raid on a journalist's home to highlight statutory limits on government seizure of reporters' materials and the procedural protections journalists enjoy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Espionage Act of 1917 (as a limit on disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Makes it illegal to obtain information relating to national defense with the intent of using that information against the United States for the gain of any foreign nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as a statutory counterpoint to press-protection doctrines — a law under which authorities have pursued cases involving classified information disclosed to reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial remedy: temporary restraining orders to protect journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts can issue temporary restraining orders (TROs) to bar federal agents from using force or threatening to arrest journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites a TRO issued in Illinois that 'bar[red] federal agents from using force or threatening to arrest journalists in Chicago', illustrating courts' role in protecting press activity during enforcement operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press freedom / safety expectation from advocacy groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements and expectations by press-freedom organizations that 'all journalists should be able to do their work safely' and that 'journalism is not a crime.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed by groups (Reporters Without Borders, ACLU, National Press Club, PEN America, etc.) and foreign ministries in reaction to incidents; used in the article as normative criteria to evaluate government conduct toward reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of law-enforcement practices toward journalists (detention, credential photography, use of force)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices criticized include detaining journalists, photographing credentials, pepper-spraying, firing less-lethal projectiles at reporters, and other actions that impede newsgathering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents criticism (e.g., Reporters Committee condemning credential-photography; State Patrol agreeing to stop detaining/photographing journalists) and tallies incidents where reporters were arrested, injured, or had equipment searched; these practices are presented as negative indicators of respect for press freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment criterion: whether federal/state officers deliberately targeted journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination by press-freedom groups and others whether officers 'appear to have deliberately targeted journalists who were doing nothing more than their job covering the news.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an evaluative standard in the article (e.g., statements by the Committee to Protect Journalists, First Amendment Coalition) to judge the propriety of enforcement actions during protests and operations.
